opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a funny path, because I started out in physics — I did my PhD in statistical physics and spent time working on superconductivity and quantum materials — and then I actually went to law school and worked as a patent attorney for a while before coming back to machine learning. So I've seen knowledge from a few very different angles.

In physics, one thing that really struck me is how open the culture is. You have arXiv, which the physics community basically pioneered. Everyone posts preprints and shares results early, and there's a sense that knowledge belongs to the community. If you want to understand a result, you can usually read the paper, and often you can reproduce the derivation yourself with pen and paper.

But even there, there were limits. Large experimental setups or big simulation codes weren't always shared, and you'd hit a wall where you just couldn't verify something without access to the same lab or the same code. Then in the patent world I saw the other extreme: knowledge treated explicitly as property, something you fence off, license, and defend.

Coming into machine learning, and especially into the early days of Hugging Face, I felt we were at a crossroads between those two cultures. Deep learning research was moving incredibly fast, but a lot of the value was in the code, the trained weights, and the data, not just the paper. A paper describing a model you can't run is a bit like a physics result you can't reproduce. It's only half of the knowledge.

So that shaped a strong conviction for me: real access to scientific knowledge means access to the artifacts — the models, datasets, and tools — not just the descriptions. That's a big part of why we open-sourced libraries like Transformers and why we've pushed so hard on open models and open datasets. It's an attempt to bring that open, community-driven spirit from physics into AI, where the stakes for who gets access are arguably even higher.

r001.rationale: The response describes missing access to labs, code, models, and data as a barrier to verification and reproduction, but does not identify access to prior scientific knowledge as a bottleneck to further discovery.

r002.rationale: It says papers can describe models that readers cannot run and that results may be unverifiable without access to the same lab or code, making clear that papers can omit artifacts needed for reproduction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it took me a long time to realize what I actually believed about this, and it came from the gap between those two worlds.

I started in physics, did a PhD in statistical physics, and physics is a field with an enormous shared culture of openness. You post your preprint on arXiv, everyone reads it, nobody waits for the journal. The whole community operates on the assumption that knowledge circulates first and gets credit second. And that felt completely natural to me. I didn't even notice it was a choice.

Then I took a detour. I actually left research and worked as a patent attorney for several years, which is an unusual path. And that was a real education, because you are sitting on the other side. You're watching companies decide very deliberately what to lock up and what to disclose, and you see how much of the innovation ecosystem runs on controlled access rather than open access. I don't think that's evil, it's just a very different model, and seeing it from the inside made me understand that openness is not the default state of the world. It has to be built and defended.

When I came back and moved into machine learning, what struck me was that this field was somewhere in between. There was a strong preprint culture, a strong open source culture, people shared code. But the actual artifacts that mattered more and more, the trained models, the datasets, the compute, those were concentrating in a very small number of places. You could read the paper, but you couldn't reproduce it. And to me, coming from physics, a result you can't reproduce isn't really science yet. It's a claim.

So I think my view of access got shaped by seeing that reading about knowledge and being able to act on it are two different things. In physics, the paper was mostly enough, you could re-derive it with a pencil. In modern AI, the paper is the tip of the iceberg. If the weights, the data, and the tooling aren't accessible, then access to the knowledge is partly an illusion. And that's really what pushed me, and a lot of us at Hugging Face, to focus not just on open publication but on open artifacts. Making the thing itself available, not just the description of it.

The other piece, which I feel strongly about, is who gets to participate. In physics, a graduate student in a small department in a country with limited funding could still contribute to theory. The barrier was mostly intellectual. I'd like AI to retain that property, and it's not guaranteed. If progress requires resources that only a handful of organizations have, we lose an enormous amount of talent and an enormous diversity of ideas. So access, for me, is not only about transparency or about being able to check results. It's about keeping the door open so that the next good idea can come from anywhere.

r001.rationale: The response says that limited access to AI artifacts makes knowledge access an illusion and can keep the next good idea from emerging anywhere, presenting access as a constraint on further discovery.

r002.rationale: It says that papers can be read while results remain unreproducible because the weights, data, and tooling needed to act on the research are unavailable.

astra-6.text:
Coming from physics, I was used to a culture where sharing knowledge was a very natural part of doing research. You could read papers and follow how an idea developed. But moving into computer science made me think more carefully about what access actually means. Being able to read about a result isn’t necessarily the same as being able to reproduce it or build on it.

In machine learning, for example, a paper is only part of the picture. You also need code, data, models, and enough computing resources to experiment. If those pieces are missing, knowledge can be publicly available in principle but still inaccessible in practice.

So I think those two perspectives complement each other: science needs ideas to circulate, and engineering gives us ways to make those ideas usable. For me, opening up scientific knowledge means helping people participate—to test a claim, change something, and contribute their own discoveries.

r001.rationale: The response says knowledge can be publicly available yet inaccessible in practice, making it harder to experiment, build on results, and contribute discoveries.

r002.rationale: It explains that reading a paper alone may not enable reproduction and names missing code, data, models, or computing resources as practical pieces needed to experiment.

sol-6.1.text:
Coming from physics, I was used to a culture where people shared their findings through papers and preprints. You could read about an idea, understand the argument, and try to build on it. That shaped my sense that scientific knowledge should be accessible, rather than something available only within a particular institution.

In computer science, and especially in machine learning, you discover that access to the paper is only part of the story. You may also need the code, the data, and the trained model to reproduce a result or explore it yourself. So openness has to extend to those things, too.

For me, the connection is that science progresses when more people can participate. Making something public is a first step, but making it usable—with tools and documentation—is what allows someone to ask a new question or take the work in a direction you hadn’t anticipated.

r001.rationale: The response says access to scientific knowledge should extend beyond institutions and that science progresses when more people can participate and build on prior work, identifying limited access as a barrier to discovery.

r002.rationale: It says access to a paper alone may be insufficient to reproduce a result, since code, data, and a trained model may also be needed.
